newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Ex-aide describes routed Afghan leader's flight.
newsitem.headline: Ex-aide describes routed Afghan leader's flight.

text.p: Afghan opposition leader Abdul Rashid Dostum fled to neighbouring Uzbekistan before going on to Turkey after losing his northern fiefdom to his opponents on Saturday, a general said on Sunday.

"He crossed the border last night with his brother and four other people," General Mahkampash, who joined last week's mutiny against Dostum, told reporters on the sun-scorched road between Mazar-i-Sharif and the Uzbek frontier town of Termez.

Dostum's party flew by helicopters from his military headquarters at Shibargham, 130 km (81 miles) west of Mazar-i-Sharif, on Saturday morning, landed in the northern capital and then headed to the Uzbek border, 90 km (56 miles) in the north, he said.
A Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesman said Dostum had arrived in Ankara on Sunday morning, but gave no details.
"His ignominous departure showed how far his support had crumbled in his ethnic Uzbek heartland," Mahkampash said.
Once a general for the former communist government, Dostum and his much feared Uzbek troops switched sides in April 1992, allowing anti-Soviet Islamic guerrillas to take over Kabul.
He rebelled against then President Buhanuddin Rabbani in 1994, but again allied with Rabbani and his military chief Ahmed Shah Masood after Taleban captured Kabul in September.
Dostum's power collapsed last week when his deputy General Abdul Malik joined forces with Taleban, along with thousands of troops and large stocks of military equipment.
"Now there is no fighting in the north, from Badghis (province) to Baghlan (province)," one of Malik's commanders, General Majid Rouzi, told reporters at the post office in Mazar-i-Sharif.
Masood still holds part of the northeast while the Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat militia has resisted Taleban attacks on its bastion of Bamiyan in central Afghanistan.
"We suggest Masood and Rabbani surrender," Rouzi said. "We are ready for talks. We are also ready for war."
Rouzi, a native of Balkh province, of which Mazar-i-Sharif is the capital, said the Jumbish-i-Milli faction once led by Dostum would continue to rule the north under new leadership.
"We will have our own power, our own weapons and will control everything until an Islamic government is established," he said.
"Dostum could not bring peace or an Islamic government to northern Afghanistan. That's why the people rejected him."

Rouzi, wearing a grey turban, said authority flowed for the moment from an eight-man military shoora (council) led by Malik's brother Gul Muhammad along with Mullah Abdul Razzaq, the hardline Taleban governor of the western province of Herat.
Rouzi said the council consisted of four representatives each of the Taleban and Jumbish, including himself.
He dismissed concerns voiced by Russian and some Central Asian states about Taleban's Islamic militancy pouring across their borders.
"Our policy is one of non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries," Rouzi said.

Most foreign diplomats and consulates in Mazar-i-Sharif have left the city in the past two days. The Pakistanis, Uzbeks and Russians departed on Saturday. A convoy from the Turkish consulate headed for Termez midday on Sunday.
